chunks: With this chain of narrators, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon them both), that he said:

Ali ibn Muhammad (peace be upon them both) entered upon a sick man from his companions while he was weeping and grieving over death, so he said to him: O servant of Allah, you fear death because you do not know it. Tell me, if you became dirty, filthy, and harmed by the abundance of dirt and grime upon you, and ulcers and scabies afflicted you, and you knew that washing in a bath would remove all of that, would you not want to enter it and wash that away from yourself, or would you dislike not entering it so that it remains upon you? He said: Yes, O son of Allah's Messenger. He said: That is death; it is that bath, and it is the last thing remaining upon you of purifying your sins and cleansing you from your misdeeds. So when you approach it and cross it, you will certainly be saved from every sorrow, anxiety, and pain, and you will reach every joy and happiness. Then the man calmed down, submitted, became eager, closed the eye of his self, and departed on his way.
ai.seo_question: What is the analogy of death as a bath in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Mani al-Akhbar*, Imam Ali ibn Muhammad (AS) employs the metaphor of a bathhouse to reframe death not as a terrifying end, but as a purifying transition that washes away the soul's accumulated sins and worldly afflictions. This perspective, rooted in Shia eschatology, encourages believers to view death as a necessary cleansing process that leads to ultimate salvation and eternal joy, thereby transforming grief into spiritual readiness.
